title: Neurohistology & Frontier Methods
summary: Apply histology to the brain and spinal cord, neurosurgical pathology and the newest tissue-imaging technologies.

lessons.title: Cerebral & Cerebellar Cortex Layers

levels.kid:
Your brain has a thin, wrinkly outer skin called the **cortex**. It is only about as thick as two or three coins stacked up. Under a microscope it looks like a layer cake.

The big main brain, the **cerebrum**, has **six layers**. Each layer has its own job. One layer listens to messages coming in from your eyes and skin. Another layer sends orders down to your muscles.

The little brain at the back, the **cerebellum**, helps you balance and move smoothly. Its cortex has only **three layers**. In the middle sits a row of big, bushy cells called **Purkinje cells**. They look like tiny trees.

The cerebellum is small, but it holds most of the brain's nerve cells!
levels.hs:
The **cerebral cortex** is the folded gray matter on the brain's surface, about 2 to 4 mm thick. Most of it is **neocortex**, which has **six layers** numbered from the surface inward:
- **I, molecular layer**: mostly fibers and dendrites, few cells.
- **II, external granular layer**: small, round neurons.
- **III, external pyramidal layer**: medium pyramidal neurons that connect cortex to cortex.
- **IV, internal granular layer**: receives sensory input from the **thalamus**.
- **V, internal pyramidal layer**: large pyramidal neurons that send output to the brainstem and spinal cord.
- **VI, multiform layer**: varied cells, many projecting back to the thalamus.

A **pyramidal neuron** has a triangular cell body and a long dendrite pointing toward the surface.

Real example: in the **primary motor cortex** (precentral gyrus), layer V holds giant **Betz cells**, whose axons run down the spinal cord to control movement. Layer IV is almost missing there, because this area mainly sends commands.

The **cerebellar cortex** has three layers:
- **Molecular layer** (outer): fibers and a few small cells.
- **Purkinje cell layer**: one row of large neurons with fan-shaped dendrites.
- **Granular layer** (inner): packed with tiny **granule cells**.

Purkinje cells are the only output of the cerebellar cortex.
levels.college:
**Neocortex** (isocortex) makes up about 90% of the human cortex. Its six layers are seen with three classic stains: **Nissl** (cell bodies), **Golgi** (whole individual neurons) and **myelin** stains (fiber bands).

Cell types:
- **Pyramidal cells** are excitatory (glutamate) and are the main projection neurons. Layer II/III pyramids send **corticocortical** and callosal axons; layer V sends **subcortical** output (corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticostriatal); layer VI sends **corticothalamic** feedback.
- **Interneurons** are mostly inhibitory (GABA), including basket and chandelier cells.
- **Spiny stellate cells** in layer IV receive thalamocortical input.

Layer thickness varies by function:
- **Granular (koniocortex)**: sensory areas such as primary visual cortex (area 17), with a very thick layer IV. In area 17, the outer **band of Baillarger** in layer IV is so prominent it is visible by eye as the **stria of Gennari**.
- **Agranular**: motor cortex (area 4), with thin or indistinct layer IV and a thick layer V with **Betz cells**.

**Korbinian Brodmann** (1909) used these laminar differences (cytoarchitecture) to map 52 areas, numbers still in use.

**Allocortex** (hippocampus, olfactory cortex) has only three layers.

**Cerebellar cortex**:
- **Molecular layer**: Purkinje dendrites, **parallel fibers** (granule cell axons), and inhibitory **stellate** and **basket cells**.
- **Purkinje cell layer**: large GABAergic neurons, flanked by **Bergmann glia**.
- **Granular layer**: granule cells (glutamatergic), Golgi cells, and **cerebellar glomeruli**, where **mossy fiber** rosettes contact granule dendrites.

Inputs: **mossy fibers** (from pontine nuclei, spinal cord and other sources) reach granule cells; **climbing fibers** from the **inferior olive** wrap each Purkinje cell. Purkinje axons inhibit the **deep cerebellar nuclei** and vestibular nuclei.
levels.phd:
Lamination arises developmentally. Neocortical excitatory neurons are born from radial glia in the ventricular and subventricular zones and migrate along radial glial fibers in an **inside-out** sequence: deep layers (VI, V) form first, and later-born neurons pass them to settle more superficially. **Cajal-Retzius cells** in the marginal zone (future layer I) secrete **reelin**, which signals through VLDLR/ApoER2 and Dab1 to stop migration. In the **reeler** mouse, lamination is roughly inverted. Human migration disorders include **lissencephaly** from *LIS1* (PAFAH1B1) or *DCX* mutations, producing a thick, poorly layered cortex.

Laminar identity has a transcription-factor code: *SATB2* (callosal neurons), *CUX2* (upper layers), *RORB* (layer IV), *BCL11B/CTIP2* and *FEZF2* (subcerebral layer V), *TBR1* and *FOXP2* (layer VI corticothalamic). Interneurons arrive differently, migrating tangentially from the ganglionic eminences.

The columnar view, from **Mountcastle** (somatosensory) and **Hubel and Wiesel** (ocular dominance columns in V1), treats cortex as repeated vertical modules spanning layers. The canonical circuit (thalamus to IV, to II/III, to V/VI) is a useful simplification; thalamic axons also contact layers V/VI directly, and in V1 layer IV is subdivided (IVA, IVB, IVCα and IVCβ receiving magnocellular and parvocellular streams).

The **cerebellum** holds roughly 69 of the brain's ~86 billion neurons (Herculano-Houzel), mostly granule cells. **Ramón y Cajal's** Golgi studies defined its circuit, later formalized by **Eccles, Ito and Szentágothai** (1967). Each Purkinje cell receives on the order of 100,000 or more parallel fiber synapses but typically one climbing fiber, which evokes a **complex spike**. The **Marr-Albus-Ito** theory proposes climbing fibers act as error signals driving **long-term depression** at parallel fiber synapses, a basis for motor learning. Purkinje cells are arranged in parasagittal **zebrin II (aldolase C)** stripes. In infancy a transient **external granular layer** lies on the surface; granule precursors proliferate there under Purkinje-derived Sonic hedgehog, then migrate inward past Purkinje cells.
levels.expert:
In surgical and autopsy neuropathology, laminar architecture is diagnostic information.

**Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD)** is a leading cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy treated by resection. The ILAE classification (2011, updated 2022) separates type I (abnormal radial or tangential lamination), type II (IIa with **dysmorphic neurons**, IIb adding **balloon cells**), and type III (dysplasia next to another lesion such as hippocampal sclerosis or a tumor). Type II is linked to somatic mTOR-pathway variants (*MTOR*, *DEPDC5*, *TSC1/2*). Judging type I needs well-oriented sections perpendicular to the pial surface; tangential cuts make normal cortex look disorganized, a common pitfall. **NeuN** immunostaining clarifies lamination, and non-phosphorylated neurofilament (SMI-32) highlights dysmorphic neurons.

**Selective vulnerability**:
- Global hypoxia-ischemia causes **laminar (pseudolaminar) necrosis**, preferentially layers III, V and VI, plus hippocampal CA1 and **Purkinje cells**. Early injured neurons appear as shrunken, hypereosinophilic "**red neurons**" (roughly 12 to 24 hours after injury).
- Chronic alcohol use is associated with Purkinje loss in the **anterior superior vermis**, giving gait ataxia.
- Spinocerebellar ataxias and essential tremor show Purkinje loss, **axonal torpedoes** and proliferation of **Bergmann glia**. Empty baskets (basket-cell fibers without a Purkinje cell) mark prior loss; calbindin staining helps count survivors.
- In ALS, Betz cells in layer V are lost.

**Recent advances**: single-nucleus RNA sequencing (Allen Institute, BRAIN Initiative Cell Census) has catalogued over a hundred cortical cell types. Human layer II/III pyramidal neurons show specializations absent in rodents, including dendritic calcium action potentials (Gidon et al., 2020). Work in mice (Yamawaki et al., 2014) identified a functional layer IV in "agranular" motor cortex, so "agranular" is better read as reduced, not absent. Layer-resolved fMRI at 7 tesla now separates feedforward from feedback signals in humans.

**Open questions**: whether the cortical column is a true computational unit, how far cerebellar computation extends to cognition and emotion (cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome), and how human-specific cell types relate to disease risk.

keyPoints: Neocortex has six layers: I molecular to VI multiform
Layer IV receives thalamic input; layer V sends subcortical output (Betz cells)
Sensory cortex is granular; motor cortex is agranular
Brodmann mapped 52 areas by cytoarchitecture
Cerebellar cortex: molecular, Purkinje cell and granular layers
Purkinje cells are GABAergic, the sole cerebellar cortex output

test.q: How many layers does typical neocortex have?
test.explain: Neocortex (isocortex) has six layers. Three layers is typical of allocortex and cerebellar cortex.

test.q: Which neocortical layer chiefly receives sensory input from the thalamus?
test.explain: Layer IV, the internal granular layer, is the main thalamic recipient. Layer VI sends feedback to the thalamus rather than being its main target.

test.q: Giant Betz cells of the motor cortex sit in which layer?
test.explain: Betz cells are large layer V pyramidal neurons whose axons join the corticospinal tract.

test.q: Which cerebellar layer lies between the molecular and granular layers?
test.explain: A single row of Purkinje cell bodies separates the outer molecular layer from the inner granular layer.

test.q: Purkinje cells release which neurotransmitter onto the deep cerebellar nuclei?
test.explain: Purkinje cells are inhibitory GABAergic neurons. Granule cells, by contrast, use glutamate.

test.q: Climbing fibers to the cerebellar cortex arise from the:
test.explain: Climbing fibers come from the inferior olive. Pontine nuclei send mossy fibers instead.

test.q: Which area is a classic example of agranular cortex?
test.explain: Motor cortex (area 4) has a thin or indistinct layer IV and a thick layer V. Sensory areas are granular.

test.q: The stria of Gennari, visible by eye, is a feature of:
test.explain: The stria of Gennari is the prominent outer band of Baillarger in layer IV of primary visual cortex (area 17).

test.q: During neocortical development, which cortical plate neurons settle into their final layer first?
choices: Upper-layer neurons of II and III
Neurons of layers II to VI at once
Deep-layer neurons of V and VI
test.explain: Cortical plate lamination is inside-out. Deep-layer neurons (VI, then V) arrive first, and later-born neurons migrate past them to form layers IV, III and II. Cajal-Retzius cells of the marginal zone (future layer I) arise even earlier, in the preplate, but they are not cortical plate neurons.

test.q: Which German anatomist mapped 52 cortical areas by cytoarchitecture in 1909?
test.explain: Korbinian Brodmann's numbered areas, such as area 4 and area 17, are still used today.

test.q: In the granular layer, mossy fiber rosettes contact granule cell dendrites in structures called cerebellar ___.
test.explain: Cerebellar glomeruli join mossy fiber terminals, granule dendrites and Golgi cell axons.

test.q: Which tiny neuron type, packed in the cerebellum's inner layer, is the most numerous neuron in the brain?
test.explain: Cerebellar granule cells make up most of the brain's neurons; their axons form parallel fibers.

kidTest.q: How many layers does the big main brain's cortex have?
kidTest.explain: The cerebrum's cortex has six layers, like a layer cake.

kidTest.q: What does the cerebellum help you do?
choices: Digest the food in your stomach
kidTest.explain: The cerebellum at the back of the brain helps you keep your balance and move smoothly.

kidTest.q: How many layers does the cerebellum's cortex have?
kidTest.explain: The cerebellar cortex has three layers.

kidTest.q: What do Purkinje cells look like?
kidTest.explain: Purkinje cells have big branching dendrites that look like little trees.

kidTest.q: The thin, wrinkly outer skin of the brain is the c _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The cortex is the brain's outer layer of gray matter.

advancedTest.q: In the reeler mouse, neocortical layers are roughly inverted. The best explanation is that without reelin:
choices: Thalamic axons arrive early and redirect neurons toward the ventricle
Radial glia stop producing new neurons before the upper layers are formed
Interneurons from the ganglionic eminences displace pyramidal cells outward
Later-born neurons fail to migrate past earlier-born neurons and stack beneath them
advancedTest.explain: Reelin from Cajal-Retzius cells guides inside-out migration. Without it, newer neurons cannot pass older ones, so the order flips.

advancedTest.q: A cortical biopsy shows no distinct layer IV and very large pyramidal neurons in layer V. The most likely source is the:
choices: Calcarine cortex of the occipital lobe
Precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
Postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
advancedTest.explain: Agranular cortex with Betz cells is primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus. The other options are granular sensory areas.

advancedTest.q: If Purkinje cells degenerate, the deep cerebellar nuclei would most directly experience:
choices: Loss of their main inhibitory input
Loss of their climbing fiber excitation
advancedTest.explain: Purkinje cells are GABAergic and inhibit the deep nuclei, so their loss disinhibits these nuclei. Parallel fibers end on Purkinje cells, not the nuclei.

advancedTest.q: A pathologist reports 'disorganized lamination' in a resected epilepsy specimen but notes the block was cut tangential to the pia. The key concern is that:
choices: Tangential sections reliably exaggerate balloon cell numbers in type IIb
Oblique cuts can make normal cortex look disorganized, mimicking FCD type I
NeuN staining fails in tangential sections, hiding neurons in layer IV
Tangential cuts remove layer I, so Cajal-Retzius cells look ectopic
advancedTest.explain: Judging FCD type I needs sections perpendicular to the pial surface. Tangential cuts distort layers and can falsely suggest dyslamination.

lessons.title: Spinal Cord, Meninges & Choroid Plexus

levels.kid:
Your spinal cord is like a thick telephone cable running down your back. It carries messages between your brain and your body.

If you cut it across and look under a microscope, you see a pattern like a **butterfly**. The butterfly shape is **gray matter**, where nerve cells live. Around it is **white matter**, made of long wires wrapped in a fatty coat, a bit like insulated cords.

The brain and cord are wrapped in three blankets called **meninges**. The outer one is tough, the middle one is like a spider web, and the inner one hugs the brain tightly.

Deep inside the brain are tiny frilly bits called the **choroid plexus**. They make a clear liquid that cushions your brain like water around a floating toy.
levels.hs:
The **spinal cord** carries signals between the brain and body. In a cross section stained for microscopy, it has two zones:
- **Gray matter**: a central H- or butterfly-shaped area full of neuron cell bodies. The **dorsal (posterior) horns** receive sensory input; the **ventral (anterior) horns** contain large **motor neurons** whose axons go to skeletal muscles.
- **White matter**: surrounding bundles of **myelinated axons** (tracts) running up and down. Myelin is fatty, which makes this area look pale in fresh tissue.

In the middle sits the tiny **central canal**, lined by **ependymal cells**.

The brain and cord are covered by three **meninges**:
- **Dura mater**: thick, tough dense connective tissue.
- **Arachnoid mater**: a thin layer with web-like strands.
- **Pia mater**: a delicate layer stuck to the surface of the nervous tissue.

Between the arachnoid and pia is the **subarachnoid space**, filled with **cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)**.

CSF is made mainly by the **choroid plexus**, frilly tufts of capillaries covered by a special epithelium that hang into the brain's ventricles. Adults make roughly 500 mL of CSF per day, replacing the whole volume several times daily.

Real example: in a **lumbar puncture**, a needle is placed below where the cord ends (around L1-L2 in adults) to sample CSF from the subarachnoid space, helping diagnose meningitis.
levels.college:
**Spinal cord cross section.** Gray matter is central, white matter peripheral (the reverse of the cerebral cortex). Key features:
- **Ventral horn**: large multipolar alpha motor neurons with abundant Nissl substance (rough ER) and a prominent nucleolus.
- **Dorsal horn**: smaller neurons; the **substantia gelatinosa** (lamina II) processes pain and temperature input.
- **Lateral horn**: present at T1-L2, containing preganglionic sympathetic neurons.
- White matter is divided into **dorsal, lateral and ventral funiculi**. The dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) carry fine touch and proprioception.
- **Rexed laminae** I-X subdivide gray matter by cytoarchitecture.

Regional identification: cervical and lumbar **enlargements** have large ventral horns serving the limbs; thoracic cord has slender horns plus lateral horns; white matter is greatest cervically because ascending tracts accumulate and descending tracts have not yet terminated.

**Meninges.**
- **Dura**: dense irregular collagen. Around the brain it is fused to periosteum; in the spine an **epidural space** with fat and venous plexus separates it from bone.
- **Arachnoid**: an outer **arachnoid barrier cell layer** joined by tight junctions, with collagen trabeculae crossing the subarachnoid space.
- **Pia**: thin, closely applied, following vessels inward. It forms **denticulate ligaments** anchoring the cord laterally. Beneath it, astrocyte endfeet form the **glia limitans**.

**Choroid plexus.** Found in the lateral, third and fourth ventricles. Each villus has:
- a core of loose connective tissue with **fenestrated capillaries**;
- a covering of **simple cuboidal epithelium** (modified ependyma) with apical microvilli and **tight junctions**, forming the **blood-CSF barrier**.

The epithelium secretes CSF actively, using apical Na+/K+-ATPase (unusually placed apically), carbonic anhydrase and aquaporin-1. CSF flows from the ventricles to the subarachnoid space and drains through **arachnoid granulations** into the dural venous sinuses.
levels.phd:
**Cord cytoarchitecture.** Rexed (1952, cat) defined ten laminae: I (marginal zone, projection neurons for the spinothalamic tract), II (substantia gelatinosa, dense small interneurons, unmyelinated C-fiber input), III-IV (nucleus proprius), V (wide-dynamic-range neurons), VII (Clarke's nucleus at C8-L3, interneurons and intermediolateral column), IX (motor pools arranged somatotopically: medial pools for axial muscles, lateral for distal limbs, flexors dorsal to extensors) and X around the central canal. Alpha motor neurons reach soma diameters above 50 µm and are flanked by smaller gamma motor neurons innervating muscle spindles. In adults the central canal is frequently obliterated by ependymal clusters, a normal age-related change rather than pathology.

**Meningeal fine structure.** The dura-arachnoid interface contains a **dural border cell layer**: flattened cells with few junctions and little extracellular collagen. This is a structural weak plane, so the "subdural space" is not preexisting but is created by cleavage, for example by hemorrhage. The arachnoid barrier layer (claudin-11, E-cadherin) provides the CSF-blood barrier on the outer side. Meningothelial cells express EMA and SSTR2A and form whorls and **psammoma bodies**, features recapitulated by meningiomas. Recent work proposed a fourth layer, **SLYM** (subarachnoid lymphatic-like membrane, Møllgård et al., 2023, Prox1+). Its existence as a discrete barrier is disputed.

**Choroid plexus physiology.** Plexus epithelium is polarized unusually: Na+/K+-ATPase and NKCC1 sit apically, and Cl−/HCO3− exchangers (AE2) sit basolaterally. Steffensen et al. (2018) argued that apical NKCC1 cotransports water directly, challenging purely osmotic models. Transthyretin is a major plexus-synthesized protein, carrying thyroxine into CSF. Epithelial cells also express Kl (klotho) and transporters clearing drugs and metabolites from CSF. **Epiplexus (Kolmer) cells** are resident macrophages on the apical surface. The plexus stroma hosts immune cells, making it a gateway for T-cell entry into the CNS.

**Drainage controversy.** The classic view had arachnoid granulations as the main CSF exit. Current evidence also supports drainage through cribriform-nasal lymphatics and dural **meningeal lymphatic vessels** (Louveau et al., 2015; Aspelund et al., 2015). The relative contributions in humans remain unresolved.
levels.expert:
**Regional level-finding in surgical pathology.** Biopsies and resected cord rarely arrive labeled by level. Combine gray/white ratio, horn shape and the presence of lateral horns or Clarke's nucleus to identify the level. A **filum terminale** specimen (from tethered-cord release) shows fibrous pia with ependymal rests and sometimes fat; this explains why **myxopapillary ependymoma** arises there.

**Meningeal pathology correlates.**
- **Epidural vs subdural hematoma**: epidural blood separates periosteal dura from skull, usually arterial (middle meningeal). Subdural blood splits the dural border cell layer and comes from bridging veins. Chronic subdurals develop neomembranes with fragile sinusoidal capillaries that rebleed, which is the rationale for **middle meningeal artery embolization**, now supported by randomized trials (EMBOLISE, MAGIC-MT, STEM; 2024).
- **Arachnoid cap cells** of granulations, clustered near the dural sinuses, falx and skull base, are the cells of origin of meningiomas. This explains their parasagittal and sphenoid wing predilection.
- Postinflammatory **arachnoiditis** and syringomyelia reflect fibrosis of the subarachnoid trabecular space disrupting CSF flow.

**Choroid plexus in neurosurgical practice.**
- Normal plexus can mimic papilloma on frozen section. Papilloma shows crowding, stratification and loss of the cobblestone apical profile, while calcified psammomatous concretions are normal with age.
- **Hydrocephalus**: most cases reflect impaired flow or absorption rather than oversecretion. Exceptions include plexus papilloma and hyperplasia. **Endoscopic third ventriculostomy with choroid plexus cauterization (ETV/CPC)**, popularized by Warf in Uganda, reduces shunt dependence in infants by ablating secretory epithelium.
- Posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus involves plexus inflammation: Karimy et al. (2017) showed TLR4/SPAK-driven NKCC1 hypersecretion. This makes CSF hypersecretion a drug target, but bumetanide's poor CNS penetration limits translation.

**Open questions.** Is SLYM a true barrier or an arachnoid sublayer artifact? How much do meningeal lymphatics matter for human amyloid clearance and neuroinflammation? Can the plexus-CSF interface be used for gene and cell delivery, given AAV serotypes that transduce plexus epithelium to secrete therapeutic proteins into CSF?

keyPoints: Spinal cord: central butterfly-shaped gray matter, peripheral white matter tracts
Ventral horns hold large motor neurons; dorsal horns process sensory input
Lateral horns (T1-L2) contain preganglionic sympathetic neurons
Meninges: dura (tough), arachnoid (web-like, barrier layer), pia (on the surface)
CSF fills the subarachnoid space and drains via arachnoid granulations and lymphatics
Choroid plexus: cuboidal epithelium with tight junctions over fenestrated capillaries forms the blood-CSF barrier

test.q: In a spinal cord cross section, where is the gray matter located?
test.explain: Spinal cord gray matter is central and butterfly-shaped, the reverse of the cerebral cortex, where gray matter is outside.

test.q: Large multipolar motor neurons supplying skeletal muscle are found in the:
test.explain: Alpha motor neurons sit in the ventral (anterior) horn. The dorsal horn is sensory and the lateral horn is sympathetic.

test.q: A cord section shows lateral horns and slender ventral horns. Which region is it most likely from?
test.explain: Lateral horns occur at T1-L2, and the thoracic cord has thin horns because it does not serve limbs.

test.q: Which meningeal layer is closely applied to the surface of the brain and cord?
test.explain: The pia mater adheres directly to the neural tissue and follows vessels inward.

test.q: Cerebrospinal fluid circulates around the brain mainly within the:
test.explain: CSF fills the subarachnoid space between the arachnoid and pia. The epidural space contains fat and veins.

test.q: What type of epithelium covers the choroid plexus?
test.explain: Choroid plexus epithelium is simple cuboidal modified ependyma with apical microvilli.

test.q: What forms the blood-CSF barrier in the choroid plexus?
choices: Collagen fibers of the dura mater
test.explain: Plexus capillaries are fenestrated and leaky. The barrier is made by tight junctions in the epithelium.

test.q: Why is a lumbar puncture performed below about L1-L2 in adults?
choices: CSF is produced at that level
The spinal cord ends above that level
The meninges are absent below it
The dura ends at that level
test.explain: The adult cord ends near L1-L2, so a needle placed lower reaches CSF without striking the cord.

test.q: Where is CSF classically absorbed into the blood?
test.explain: Arachnoid granulations drain CSF into the dural venous sinuses. The choroid plexus produces CSF rather than absorbing it.

test.q: The central canal of the spinal cord is lined by ___ cells.
test.explain: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal.

test.q: What is the middle, web-like meningeal layer called?
test.explain: The arachnoid sends web-like trabeculae across the subarachnoid space.

test.q: The dorsal horn region called the substantia ___ processes pain and temperature signals.
test.explain: The substantia gelatinosa (Rexed lamina II) receives unmyelinated pain fibers.

kidTest.q: What shape does the gray matter make in a cut spinal cord?
kidTest.explain: The gray matter in the middle looks like a butterfly.

kidTest.q: What are the meninges?
kidTest.explain: The meninges are three protective coverings around the brain and spinal cord.

kidTest.q: What does the choroid plexus make?
choices: New bone tissue for the skull
kidTest.explain: It makes cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the brain.

kidTest.q: What makes white matter look pale?
choices: A fatty coat on the wires
kidTest.explain: The fatty myelin coat on the nerve wires makes white matter pale.

kidTest.q: The middle covering of the brain is like a spider's w _ _.
kidTest.explain: The arachnoid layer looks like a spider web.

advancedTest.q: Why is the 'subdural space' considered a potential space created by injury?
choices: Cerebrospinal fluid normally fills it and drains after trauma
The dural border cell layer has few junctions and splits easily
Meningeal lymphatics leave a cavity once they are disrupted
Dense collagen in the arachnoid barrier tears under pressure
advancedTest.explain: The dural border cells are loosely joined with little collagen, so bleeding cleaves this weak plane instead of filling a preexisting space.

advancedTest.q: Cervical cord has the largest white matter area. The best explanation is:
choices: Lateral horns are absent, leaving extra space for tracts
Cervical gray matter is reduced to make room for tracts
Ascending tracts have accumulated and descending ones are still intact
Cervical axons have thicker myelin than lumbar axons
advancedTest.explain: Ascending fibers add up toward the head, and descending fibers have not yet terminated, so total tract volume peaks cervically.

advancedTest.q: Choroid plexus cauterization lowers shunt need in infant hydrocephalus mainly by:
choices: Reducing CSF secretion by ablating plexus epithelium
Sealing fenestrations in the plexus capillary walls
Diverting CSF into the epidural venous plexus
Opening arachnoid granulations to increase absorption
advancedTest.explain: Cauterizing the secretory epithelium lowers CSF production, complementing third ventriculostomy, which bypasses obstruction.

advancedTest.q: Posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus findings from Karimy et al. suggested a drug target because:
choices: Blood clots blocked the arachnoid granulations
Ependymal cilia stopped beating after the hemorrhage
Hemoglobin destroyed the arachnoid barrier tight junctions
Inflammatory signaling drove NKCC1-mediated CSF hypersecretion
advancedTest.explain: TLR4/SPAK signaling increased NKCC1 activity in plexus epithelium, showing that oversecretion, not only blocked absorption, contributes and could be blocked by drugs.

lessons.title: CNS Tumor Histology & Intraoperative Frozen Sections

levels.kid:
Sometimes a lump grows inside the brain. Doctors call it a **tumor**. A brain surgeon needs to know what kind of lump it is, and fast, while the patient is still asleep in the operating room.

So the surgeon sends a tiny piece to a **pathologist**, a doctor who looks at cells. The pathologist freezes the piece until it is hard like an ice pop. Then a sharp machine slices it thinner than a hair. Pink and purple dyes make the cells easy to see.

In about 20 minutes, the pathologist calls the surgeon. "This looks like a tumor that started in the brain," or "This came from somewhere else." That quick answer helps the surgeon decide what to do next.
levels.hs:
A **CNS tumor** is an abnormal growth in the brain or spinal cord. Some start in the brain itself (**primary tumors**). Others spread there from cancers elsewhere, such as the lung or skin (**metastases**). The most common primary tumors include **gliomas**, which come from glial support cells, and **meningiomas**, which grow from the meninges, the coverings of the brain.

During surgery, the neurosurgeon often needs a diagnosis right away. The tool for this is the **intraoperative frozen section**:
- A small piece of tissue is frozen quickly in a gel.
- A freezing slicer called a **cryostat** cuts it into very thin slices.
- The slices are stained with **H&E** (hematoxylin and eosin), which colors nuclei purple and cytoplasm pink.
- A pathologist reads the slide and reports back, usually within about 20 to 30 minutes.

Neuropathologists also make a **smear** (squash prep). They press a tiny bit of soft brain tissue between two glass slides. This shows cell shapes and fine processes very well.

Example: a slide with many crowded, odd-shaped glial cells, dead tissue, and abnormal blood vessels suggests **glioblastoma**, the most aggressive glioma. If the slide shows whorls of cells instead, a meningioma is more likely. The final diagnosis comes days later from permanent sections and molecular tests.
levels.college:
Frozen sections answer intraoperative questions: Is this lesional tissue? Is it a primary CNS tumor, a metastasis, lymphoma or infection? Is there enough diagnostic tissue for the permanent workup?

**Technique.** Fresh tissue is embedded in OCT compound, snap-frozen at about −20 °C in a cryostat, cut at roughly 5–8 µm, and stained with rapid H&E. Ice-crystal artifact creates vacuoles and nuclear distortion, which can mimic edema or the clear-cell look of oligodendroglioma. **Smear/squash preparations** avoid freezing and show processes, nuclear detail and cohesion. Neuropathologists usually read both together.

**Key histologic patterns:**
- **Diffuse astrocytoma/glioblastoma**: infiltrating atypical astrocytes with fibrillary processes. Glioblastoma adds **microvascular proliferation** (glomeruloid vessels) and/or **necrosis**, classically pseudopalisading.
- **Oligodendroglioma**: round, uniform nuclei with perinuclear halos ("fried egg," a fixation artifact), chicken-wire capillaries and calcifications.
- **Meningioma**: whorls, psammoma bodies, intranuclear pseudoinclusions. Usually dural-based.
- **Metastatic carcinoma**: cohesive epithelial clusters with a sharp border against brain tissue, unlike gliomas, which infiltrate.
- **Primary CNS lymphoma**: discohesive atypical lymphocytes cuffing vessels (angiocentric). Recognizing it changes management, because resection is generally not the goal and biopsy suffices.
- **Pilocytic astrocytoma**: biphasic pattern with Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies.
- **Ependymoma**: perivascular pseudorosettes.
- **Medulloblastoma**: small round blue cells, Homer Wright rosettes.

**Integrated diagnosis.** Under the WHO CNS5 classification (2021), histology is combined with molecular markers. Examples are **IDH** mutation status, **1p/19q codeletion** (which defines oligodendroglioma), and in IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumors, **TERT promoter mutation**, **EGFR amplification** or +7/−10, which establishes glioblastoma even without necrosis.
levels.phd:
The WHO CNS5 (2021) framework replaced purely morphological grading with layered, integrated diagnoses: histology, CNS WHO grade (Arabic numerals, assigned within tumor types), molecular information, and an integrated name. Adult diffuse gliomas reduce to three families:
- **Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant**, grades 2–4. CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion confers grade 4 regardless of histology.
- **Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted**, grades 2–3.
- **Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype**, grade 4.

The term "IDH-mutant glioblastoma" was retired. Mechanistically, mutant IDH1 (classically R132H, detectable by immunohistochemistry) produces the oncometabolite **2-hydroxyglutarate**. This compound inhibits α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, including TET demethylases and JmjC histone demethylases, and drives the glioma CpG island methylator phenotype (G-CIMP). ATRX loss and TP53 mutation accompany astrocytoma. TERT promoter mutation and CIC/FUBP1 mutations accompany oligodendroglioma.

Paediatric-type tumors are separated biologically. Examples include **diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered**, in which the K27M oncohistone inhibits PRC2 and causes global loss of H3K27me3. Medulloblastoma is classified as WNT, SHH (TP53-wildtype or mutant) or non-WNT/non-SHH, and the molecular group outweighs histology in predicting prognosis.

**DNA methylation profiling** (Capper et al., Nature 2018) classifies tumors with a random-forest classifier trained on about 2,800 tumors spanning about 90 classes. In that study, profiling changed the original diagnosis in roughly 12% of cases. It is now a recommended, and sometimes defining, criterion.

Frozen-section concordance with final diagnosis in neuropathology series is roughly 90–95%. Most discordances involve grading rather than lineage. Sampling error is intrinsic: a biopsy from the infiltrating edge of a glioblastoma can look like a low-grade glioma. Gliosis versus low-grade glioma, radiation necrosis versus recurrent tumor, and demyelinating "tumefactive" lesions (macrophage-rich, mimicking glioma) are classic traps. Steroids given before surgery can make lymphoma undetectable through lympholysis. Grade cannot be reliably assigned on frozen section when the molecular criteria are what define it.
levels.expert:
Intraoperative consultation is a negotiation between the surgeon's question and what frozen tissue can actually show. The most valuable answers are binary and actionable. Is this "lesional, diagnostic tissue: stop sampling"? Is it "lymphoma: do not resect"? Is it "metastasis versus glioma"? Or is it "nondiagnostic: sample deeper, toward the enhancing rim"? Correlation with imaging is mandatory. A ring-enhancing lesion read as "gliosis" means the biopsy probably missed the target.

Pitfalls worth anticipating:
- **Freezing depletes scarce tissue.** Stereotactic biopsies should be triaged: smear plus limited frozen section, keeping cores for permanent sections and molecular testing.
- **Infection and abscess** need cultures taken intraoperatively. Clinical history (immunosuppression) should change who handles the tissue.
- **Prion disease suspicion** triggers special handling, because ordinary decontamination is inadequate. Many centers avoid freezing such tissue in the shared cryostat.

**Rapid molecular intraoperative diagnosis** is arriving. Examples include IDH1 R132H detection by fast genotyping, and nanopore-based methylation classification (e.g., the Rapid-CNS2 and Sturgeon approaches) that report methylation class within the operative window. These can tell a surgeon that a tumor is an IDH-mutant glioma, where more extensive resection improves survival, or a lymphoma, where it does not.

**Label-free optical histology** is reshaping the workflow. **Stimulated Raman histology** (SRH) images fresh, unprocessed tissue in minutes. In the prospective trial by Hollon and colleagues (Nature Medicine, 2020), a deep-learning classifier interpreting SRH matched pathologist accuracy on conventional frozen sections. Related work extends this to detecting infiltrating tumor at resection margins. This matters neurosurgically because the aim is maximal safe resection, and residual tumor at the margin determines outcome. Complementary adjuncts include **5-ALA** fluorescence, which makes high-grade glioma visible to the surgeon.

Open questions include how to validate AI and rapid-molecular calls before they drive irreversible surgical decisions, and how to communicate uncertainty in the minute-scale timeframe. A further question is whether margin assessment can become quantitative rather than impressionistic.

keyPoints: Frozen sections give a rapid intraoperative diagnosis in about 20–30 minutes
Smear (squash) preps complement frozen sections for brain tissue
Glioblastoma: necrosis and microvascular proliferation, or defining molecular markers
Metastases have sharp borders; gliomas infiltrate
WHO CNS5 integrates histology with IDH, 1p/19q and other markers
Stimulated Raman histology and rapid methylation profiling are new intraoperative tools

lessons.title: Digital Pathology & AI Slide Analysis

levels.kid:
Imagine taking a giant photo of a tiny slice of tissue, so big that you could zoom in like a map on a phone. That is what a **slide scanner** does. It snaps thousands of little pictures and stitches them together into one huge picture.

Now doctors can look at the tissue on a computer screen instead of squinting into a microscope. They can even send the picture to an expert far away in a few seconds.

Computers can also learn to spot patterns, like a very fast helper. If you show a computer thousands of pictures of healthy and sick tissue, it starts to notice the differences. But the computer is a helper, not the boss. A trained doctor still checks the answer.
levels.hs:
**Digital pathology** means turning glass microscope slides into high-resolution computer images. A machine called a **whole-slide scanner** moves the slide under a microscope lens, captures thousands of small image tiles, and stitches them into one **whole-slide image (WSI)**. One WSI can be several gigabytes, because it holds detail down to individual cells.

Why bother?
- Pathologists can view, zoom and measure slides on a screen.
- Slides can be shared instantly for a second opinion, which is called **telepathology**.
- Images never fade or break the way old glass slides can.

The second big idea is **artificial intelligence (AI)**. In **machine learning**, a computer program is trained on many labeled examples, such as slides marked "cancer" or "no cancer," until it learns the visual patterns itself. A common type is the **convolutional neural network (CNN)**, which is especially good at recognizing shapes and textures in images.

A real example: in 2021 the US FDA authorized **Paige Prostate**, the first AI software to help pathologists find suspicious areas in prostate biopsies. In studies, it helped pathologists catch small cancers they might otherwise miss.

AI does not replace the pathologist. It acts as a second pair of eyes, flagging areas to look at closely, counting cells, or measuring features. The pathologist makes the final diagnosis.
levels.college:
Digital pathology converts stained glass slides (usually H&E or immunohistochemistry) into **whole-slide images** that can be viewed, analyzed and archived computationally.

**Image acquisition.**
- Scanners capture tiles at about 20x (around 0.5 µm per pixel) or 40x (around 0.25 µm per pixel) and stitch them together.
- WSIs are stored as **image pyramids**: several resolutions of the same slide, so a viewer loads only the zoom level and region on screen.
- Focus is set at chosen points across the tissue. Thick or folded sections can blur, and **z-stacking** (several focal planes) helps with cytology but multiplies file size.
- Validation guidelines from the College of American Pathologists ask labs to show that digital diagnoses agree closely with glass diagnoses before using WSIs for primary diagnosis.

**Image analysis.**
- Classic **quantitative image analysis** uses hand-designed rules, for example thresholding brown DAB staining to score Ki-67 or HER2.
- **Color deconvolution** separates hematoxylin and eosin (or DAB) signals mathematically.
- **Deep learning** with CNNs learns features directly from pixels. Because a whole WSI is too large to process at once, it is cut into **patches** (for example 256 x 256 pixels) that are analyzed and then aggregated.

**Typical tasks.**
- Detection: metastases in lymph nodes, mitoses, small tumor foci.
- Segmentation: outlining tumor, stroma, necrosis or individual nuclei.
- Grading and scoring: Gleason patterns, Ki-67 index.
- Prediction: estimating molecular status or prognosis from morphology alone.

**Landmarks.** The **CAMELYON16** challenge (2016) showed that top algorithms could detect breast cancer metastases in sentinel lymph nodes as well as pathologists working without time limits. In 2017 the FDA cleared the Philips IntelliSite system for primary diagnosis, and in 2021 authorized Paige Prostate as the first AI pathology tool.
levels.phd:
**Weak supervision.** Pixel-level annotation of gigapixel WSIs is too expensive to do at scale, so most modern models learn from slide-level labels alone through **multiple-instance learning (MIL)**. A slide is treated as a "bag" of patch "instances." Under the standard MIL assumption, a bag is positive if at least one instance is positive. Campanella et al. (*Nature Medicine*, 2019) trained MIL models on more than 44,000 WSIs with only diagnostic-report labels and reached an AUC near 0.98 for prostate cancer, showing that clinical-scale data can replace manual outlining.

**Attention-based MIL** (Ilse et al., 2018; CLAM by Lu et al., 2021) learns a weight for each patch embedding. The weighted sum gives a slide representation, and the attention maps show which regions drove the prediction. Note that high attention means "influential," not necessarily "diagnostic."

**Foundation models.** Self-supervised learning (contrastive methods, DINOv2-style self-distillation, masked image modeling) on millions of unlabeled patches produces general-purpose encoders such as UNI, Virchow, CONCH (a vision-language model) and Prov-GigaPath. These improve label efficiency on downstream tasks, although benchmark gains vary by task and dataset.

**Morphology-to-molecule prediction.** Kather et al. (2019) predicted **microsatellite instability** in colorectal cancer directly from H&E. Coudray et al. (2018) predicted EGFR and STK11 mutations in lung adenocarcinoma. Such signals are real but often modest. They may reflect correlated phenotypes, such as the mucinous pattern and heavy lymphocyte infiltration of MSI tumors, rather than the mutation itself.

**Pitfalls in generalization.**
- **Domain shift** from staining protocols, scanners and section thickness can sharply degrade performance at outside sites.
- **Stain normalization** (Macenko, Reinhard) or color augmentation reduces but does not remove this shift.
- **Batch confounding** is a real risk: TCGA studies showed that the submitting site can be predicted from H&E alone, so models can learn site artifacts that correlate with outcomes.
- Proper evaluation needs **patient-level splits** and truly external test cohorts.
levels.expert:
**Neuropathology applications.**
- **WHO CNS5** (2021) folds molecular markers into tumor classification, such as IDH status, 1p/19q codeletion and H3 K27 alteration. Models that predict IDH mutation or glioma subtype from H&E can help triage, but they cannot replace sequencing or immunohistochemistry for integrated diagnosis.
- The **DNA methylation classifier** (Capper et al., *Nature*, 2018) is a non-imaging machine-learning tool that is already part of everyday neuropathology. Its calibrated scores, and its "no match" outputs, model good uncertainty reporting.
- **Stimulated Raman histology** combined with CNNs (Hollon et al., *Nature Medicine*, 2020) gave intraoperative brain tumor diagnoses in under about 3 minutes, comparable to frozen-section reading, without sectioning or staining. This makes the technique a true digital alternative workflow in the operating room.

**Regulatory and deployment realities.**
- FDA pathways include 510(k) and De Novo. Paige Prostate (De Novo, 2021) set a product category for later tools.
- In Europe, the IVDR raised the requirements for clinical evidence.
- **Locked versus adaptive algorithms**: continuously learning models need predetermined change-control plans.
- Integration needs a **DICOM WSI** standard, which is now maturing as an alternative to proprietary formats, plus links to laboratory information systems and enough storage (petabytes for a large department).

**Human-AI interaction risks.**
- **Automation bias**: readers defer to wrong AI calls. Studies show that assistance helps on average but can mislead on difficult cases.
- Reader-study designs (crossover with washout) matter more than the AUC of the algorithm alone.
- **Calibration** and **out-of-distribution detection** are essential. A model should flag tissue it was never trained on, such as a rare entity, rather than force it into a known class.

**Open questions.**
- Can prognostic models add value beyond grade, stage and molecular markers in prospective trials?
- Do generative models and multimodal "copilots" (for example PathChat) produce fabricated descriptions?
- How should fairness be checked across populations and institutions?
- How should liability be divided when AI-assisted diagnoses are wrong?

Convolutional neural networks learn visual features from labeled slides

AI assists the pathologist, who makes the final diagnosis

kidTest.explain: It stitches many small photos into one huge picture.

kidTest.explain: Digital slides are viewed on screens.

kidTest.explain: It learns from thousands of labeled pictures.

kidTest.q: Who checks the computer's answer?

advancedTest.explain: A bag is positive if at least one instance is positive, so a negative bag contains no positive instances. 'Most patches benign' is too weak because it leaves room for a positive patch.

advancedTest.explain: The model may rely on mucinous pattern or lymphocyte infiltration, which only correlate with MSI status.

advancedTest.explain: Real-world value depends on external validation, human-AI reader effects and calibrated uncertainty. WHO CNS5 still requires molecular confirmation, so replacing sequencing is not acceptable.

lessons.title: Spatial Omics, Tissue Clearing & Expansion Microscopy

levels.kid:
Imagine a giant city made of tiny houses. A normal map shows you where the houses are. But what if you could also see what every family inside is cooking for dinner? That is what **spatial omics** does for cells. It shows where each cell sits and which genes it is using.

Scientists have other new tricks too. **Tissue clearing** makes a whole mouse brain see-through, like turning a muddy pond into clear glass. Then you can look all the way through it.

**Expansion microscopy** is even stranger. Scientists soak tissue in a jelly like the stuff in a diaper. When they add water, the jelly swells and gently pulls the tiny parts apart, so they look bigger and easier to see.
levels.hs:
Classic histology slices tissue very thin and stains it, usually with H&E. That shows shapes beautifully, but it tells you little about which genes each cell is using, and it only shows one flat slice. Three newer methods tackle these limits.

- **Spatial omics** measures molecules while keeping track of where they sit. *Spatial transcriptomics* maps RNA, the messages copied from genes, across a tissue section. A popular tool, 10x Genomics **Visium**, puts a section on a slide covered in spots. Each spot carries a DNA **barcode**, a short tag that records the location. After sequencing, a computer rebuilds a gene-activity map of the tissue.
- **Tissue clearing** makes thick organs transparent. Tissue looks cloudy because fats and proteins bend light by different amounts. Clearing removes the fats and evens out that light-bending, measured as the **refractive index**. The method **CLARITY** (2013) made a whole mouse brain see-through, so neurons could be traced in 3D with a **light-sheet microscope**.
- **Expansion microscopy (ExM)** makes the specimen itself bigger. Tissue is linked into a swellable gel and its proteins are digested. When water is added, the gel expands about 4 times in each direction, so ordinary microscopes can see detail near 70 nanometers.

Example: researchers have used spatial transcriptomics to show how glioblastoma cells differ between the tumor core and the invading edge.
levels.college:
These frontier methods extend histology along three axes: molecular content, the third dimension, and resolution.

**Spatial transcriptomics** comes in two main families.
- **Sequencing-based** methods capture RNA from a tissue section onto barcoded arrays. In Visium, polyadenylated mRNA binds poly(dT) probes on 55 µm spots, so each spot pools roughly 1 to 10 cells. Newer versions improve on this. Slide-seq uses 10 µm beads, and Visium HD and Stereo-seq reach subcellular bins. These methods sample the whole transcriptome without choosing genes in advance.
- **Imaging-based** methods detect individual RNA molecules by repeated fluorescent hybridization. Examples include MERFISH, seqFISH, Xenium and CosMx. They give single-cell or subcellular resolution but use a preselected panel of hundreds to thousands of genes.

**Spatial proteomics** maps proteins instead. CODEX/PhenoCycler uses DNA-barcoded antibodies that are revealed in cycles. Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) uses metal-tagged antibodies read by laser ablation and mass spectrometry. Both allow about 40 or more markers on one section.

**Tissue clearing** works by matching refractive indices to reduce light scattering. Lipids are a major scatterer.
- *Organic solvent* methods such as 3DISCO and iDISCO dehydrate tissue, remove lipids and shrink it.
- *Aqueous* methods include CUBIC and Scale.
- *Hydrogel* methods such as CLARITY and PACT bind proteins to an acrylamide mesh and then wash out lipids with SDS detergent.
Cleared organs are then imaged with light-sheet microscopy.

**Expansion microscopy** (Boyden lab, 2015) works in several steps.
- Labels or native proteins are anchored to a polyacrylate gel.
- The tissue is homogenized with proteinase K.
- The gel is swelled in water about 4-fold in each direction.

The result is physical super-resolution, about 300/4 ≈ 70 nm, on a standard confocal microscope.
levels.phd:
**Resolution versus coverage** is the central tradeoff in spatial transcriptomics. Spot-based capture (Visium; Ståhl et al., *Science* 2016) yields mixtures of cells per spot. Each spot's signal therefore has to be split into estimated cell types by **deconvolution** against single-cell RNA-seq references, using tools such as cell2location, RCTD or SPOTlight. Imaging methods resolve single molecules, but they need **cell segmentation**. Errors in drawing cell boundaries leak transcripts into neighbouring cells, creating apparent co-expression that is not real. MERFISH (Chen, Zhuang et al., 2015) uses combinatorial binary barcodes with Hamming-distance error correction, which lets it multiplex beyond the number of colour channels. Its practical ceiling is set by **optical crowding** of RNA spots, which expansion can ease (ExM-MERFISH). In situ sequencing methods (STARmap, FISSEQ, ExSeq) read barcodes directly in tissue.

**Tissue clearing physics.** Opacity comes from refractive index (RI) mismatch between lipids (RI ~1.45), proteins (~1.44) and water (1.33). Methods either remove scatterers or raise the immersion medium's RI to about 1.45-1.56. CLARITY (Chung & Deisseroth, *Nature* 2013) uses formaldehyde-acrylamide hybrid hydrogels and electrophoretic SDS delipidation. Solvent methods such as iDISCO+ make whole-brain immunolabeling of the mouse brain practical. Antibody penetration remains rate-limiting because diffusion time scales roughly with the square of tissue depth. SHIELD and stochastic electrotransport help address this. Pipelines such as ClearMap register cell counts to the Allen Common Coordinate Framework.

**Expansion fidelity.** Proteinase digestion together with uniform gel chemistry gives isotropic expansion. Distortion measured against pre-expansion images is a few percent over tens of micrometres, but it must be validated for each tissue. Iterative ExM and ten-fold expansion (X10) reach about 25 nm and below. Variants include:
- **proExM**, which anchors proteins with AcX
- **U-ExM**, which preserves the ultrastructure of centrioles and cilia
- **ExR**, which labels after expansion so antibodies can reach crowded synaptic epitopes

An open controversy is **linkage error**. Antibody size of about 10-20 nm is itself magnified by expansion, and incomplete homogenization can bias which structures appear. Correlating against electron microscopy remains the reference standard.
levels.expert:
For neurosurgical and neuro-oncology research, these tools are shifting interpretation from cell type alone to cell *niche*. In glioblastoma, spatial transcriptomics combined with single-cell atlases has mapped malignant cellular states (Neftel et al., 2019) onto anatomical niches. These include hypoxic mesenchymal-like programs around pseudopalisading necrosis and neural-progenitor-like states at the infiltrative margin. Greenwald et al. (2024) proposed a layered organization linked to hypoxia. The infiltrative edge is precisely the tissue left behind after resection. Mapping it may explain recurrence and help guide intraoperative sampling.

Practical pitfalls when designing a study:
- **RNA quality.** Fresh-frozen tissue preserves RNA best, so the RNA integrity number (RIN) should be checked. FFPE protocols using probe ligation (Visium CytAssist, Xenium) now unlock archival neuropathology blocks.
- **Panel bias.** Imaging panels detect only the genes you anticipated. Pairing them with whole-transcriptome data on adjacent sections is common practice.
- **Statistics.** Spots and cells within one section are not independent samples. Patient-level replication matters more than very large cell counts.
- **Human brain clearing.** Lipofuscin autofluorescence, myelin density and long postmortem fixation all hamper human tissue. Methods such as SHANEL and new tissue-sectioning approaches allow centimetre-scale human blocks, but data reach terabytes per sample.

Recent advances include:
- **Spatial multi-omics** on the same section, combining RNA, protein and chromatin accessibility, for example spatial ATAC.
- **3D spatial transcriptomics**, built from serial sections or from cleared, thick tissue imaged by light-sheet.
- **ExM in clinical pathology** (expansion pathology, ExPath), which can resolve kidney podocyte foot processes or nanoscale pathology on standard microscopes and may reduce reliance on electron microscopy.
- **Foundation models** that predict spatial gene expression from H&E images.

Open questions remain. Can expression inferred from H&E become a validated biomarker? How should spatial data be standardized across platforms? Will rapid spatial assays ever become fast enough to inform decisions during surgery? A related community effort, the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas, now uses MERFISH-based whole-mouse-brain maps of over 5,000 transcriptomic clusters, providing reference coordinates against which human disease tissue is compared.

keyPoints: Spatial omics measures RNA or proteins while preserving location in tissue
Sequencing-based methods (Visium) cover the whole transcriptome; imaging methods (MERFISH) give single-cell resolution
Spot-based data need deconvolution; imaging data need accurate cell segmentation
Tissue clearing removes lipids and matches refractive index to make organs transparent
CLARITY uses a hydrogel and detergent; cleared tissue is imaged by light-sheet microscopy
Expansion microscopy physically swells tissue in a gel about 4-fold for ~70 nm resolution

test.q: What does spatial transcriptomics add to ordinary histology?
choices: A three-dimensional view of whole organs
A map of gene expression by location
test.explain: It measures RNA while recording where in the tissue it came from. Clearing, not spatial transcriptomics, is the method aimed at whole-organ 3D views.

test.q: In Visium, how is each RNA molecule linked to its position?
choices: By the color of a fluorescent dye
By laser ablation of metal tags
By a DNA barcode on its capture spot
By its distance from the slide edge
test.explain: Capture spots carry spatial barcodes that are read during sequencing. Metal tags and laser ablation describe imaging mass cytometry.

test.q: Why does untreated tissue look cloudy?
choices: Blood pigments block the light path
Water in cells absorbs visible light
Nuclei reflect light like small mirrors
test.explain: Mismatched refractive indices of lipids, proteins and water scatter light, so clearing removes lipids and matches indices.

test.q: Which microscope is typically used to image whole cleared organs?
test.explain: Light-sheet microscopy illuminates one plane at a time and images large transparent samples quickly.

test.q: How does expansion microscopy improve resolution?
test.explain: The tissue is embedded in a swellable gel that expands about 4-fold in each direction, so standard optics can resolve finer detail.

test.q: Which enzyme step lets expansion gels swell evenly?
test.explain: Proteinase K homogenizes the tissue's mechanical structure so it does not resist uniform swelling.

test.q: MERFISH and Xenium differ from Visium mainly because they:
choices: Measure the whole transcriptome in big spots
Image single RNAs from a chosen gene panel
Clear the tissue before taking sections
Use mass spectrometry to read proteins
test.explain: Imaging-based methods detect individual molecules at high resolution but need a preselected panel of genes.

test.q: CLARITY removes lipids from tissue using:
test.explain: CLARITY binds proteins to an acrylamide hydrogel, then washes out lipids with SDS detergent. Solvent dehydration is the DISCO approach.

test.q: Which technique maps around 40 proteins using metal-tagged antibodies?
test.explain: Imaging mass cytometry reads metal tags by laser ablation and mass spectrometry, allowing high multiplexing.

test.q: Clearing works by matching the refractive ___ of tissue and the surrounding medium.
test.explain: Matching the refractive index reduces light scattering, so tissue turns transparent.

test.q: Name the 2013 hydrogel-based method that made a whole mouse brain transparent.
test.explain: CLARITY was developed by Chung and Deisseroth and published in 2013.

test.q: Expansion microscopy enlarges tissue about ___-fold in each direction.
test.explain: A roughly 4x expansion turns a ~300 nm optical limit into ~70 nm effective resolution.

kidTest.q: What does spatial omics show about cells?
choices: How heavy each one of the cells is
How fast each of the cells can swim
Their place and the genes they use
kidTest.explain: It maps both location and gene activity, like seeing what each family in the city is cooking.

kidTest.q: What does tissue clearing do to a brain?
kidTest.explain: Clearing turns cloudy tissue transparent so scientists can look through it.

kidTest.q: In expansion microscopy, what makes the tissue bigger?
choices: A jelly that swells with water
A heater that warms it up
A tiny pump that blows air
kidTest.explain: A swellable gel, like diaper jelly, gently pulls the tiny parts apart.

kidTest.q: Why make tiny parts spread apart?
choices: So they are easier to see
kidTest.explain: Spreading parts apart lets a normal microscope see details that were too close together.

kidTest.q: Tissue clearing makes a brain look like clear g _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Cleared tissue becomes transparent, like glass.

advancedTest.q: A Visium spot shows high neuron and microglia markers together. The best interpretation is:
choices: A 55 µm spot pooling several cell types
A reverse transcription error at the spot
One hybrid cell type expressing both programs
advancedTest.explain: Spots pool roughly 1 to 10 cells, so a mixed signal usually reflects mixed cells, which deconvolution aims to resolve.

advancedTest.q: In imaging-based spatial data, apparent co-expression of exclusive markers in adjacent cells most likely reflects:
choices: Panel genes chosen with too much overlap
advancedTest.explain: Segmentation errors assign transcripts to neighbouring cells, creating false co-expression.

advancedTest.q: Why does antibody labeling of large cleared samples become slow as size increases?
choices: Diffusion time scales roughly with depth squared
Lipid content increases toward the center
Light-sheet power falls linearly with depth
Refractive index rises with tissue thickness
advancedTest.explain: Diffusion time grows with the square of distance, so doubling depth roughly quadruples labeling time.

advancedTest.q: After 10-fold expansion, why might an antibody-labeled structure appear displaced from its true position?
choices: Fluorophores bleach faster in a swollen gel
Antibody size is magnified as linkage error
Proteinase K shifts proteins along the axons
advancedTest.explain: The 10-20 nm offset between epitope and fluorophore is itself expanded, so it becomes a visible error at high expansion factors.
